tagline: A personal note from the elder to his friend Gaius, praising his hospitality to traveling missionaries and confronting Diotrephes, a church leader who loves to be first.
overview:
Third John is the shortest book in the New Testament by word count, and the most personal of John's letters. It is a private note from the elder to a man named Gaius, whom he loves in the truth. Traveling Christian workers have come back to the elder with good reports: Gaius has welcomed them, fed them, and sent them on their way, even though they were strangers to him. The elder commends this and urges him to keep doing it, because those who support such workers become fellow workers for the truth.

The letter also names a problem. Diotrephes, a leader in the church, loves to be first. He has refused the elder's letter, spread malicious talk against him, turned away the traveling brothers, and even put out of the church those who wanted to welcome them. The elder promises to deal with it when he comes. Meanwhile he commends a man named Demetrius, who very likely carried the letter.

The letter is precious for what it shows of ordinary church life at the end of the first century: travel, hospitality, money, letters, rivalries, and friendships. It shows truth and love not as abstractions but as the way believers treat strangers and handle power.
author: As in Second John, the writer calls himself the elder. Early tradition identified him with John the apostle, and the shared vocabulary of the three letters (truth, love, walking in the truth, testimony, seeing God) points to one author or circle. Some scholars identify the elder with a leader distinct from the apostle, perhaps the John the elder whom Papias mentions in the early second century. What is clear from the letter is that the elder had recognized standing over more than one congregation and expected his letters and messengers to be received, and that at least one local leader was now resisting that standing.
date: Usually dated with the other letters of John, late in the first century, around AD 85 to 100. Nothing in the letter fixes the date more precisely. It gives no sign of the doctrinal dispute that dominates First and Second John; the conflict here is about authority and hospitality.
setting:
Christian mission in the Roman world depended on hospitality. Inns were few, expensive, and often disreputable, so traveling teachers and missionaries relied on believers to house them and to send them on with supplies for the next stage. The elder notes that these workers went out for the sake of the Name and accepted nothing from the Gentiles (verse 7), meaning they did not take support from unbelievers, which set them apart from traveling philosophers and religious teachers who lived on public gifts. The Didache, a Christian manual of church practice from about the same era or a little later, gives rules for receiving traveling apostles and prophets, which shows how common and how open to abuse the system was.

We know nothing of Gaius, Diotrephes, or Demetrius beyond this letter. Gaius was one of the most common Roman names, and the New Testament mentions several men called Gaius; there is no good reason to identify this one with any of them. Whether Diotrephes held a formal office or simply dominated a house church is unclear. Scholars have read the conflict as a clash of personalities, a struggle between traveling and local leadership, or an early step toward the single presiding bishop found in the second century. The letter does not say, and it is wise not to claim more than it tells.
purpose: The elder writes to thank and encourage Gaius for his hospitality, to ask him to continue supporting traveling workers, to warn him about Diotrephes' conduct and signal that the elder will address it in person, and to commend Demetrius. Underneath these practical aims is a single conviction: walking in the truth shows itself in how believers welcome others.
story: Third John belongs to the same period and circle as First and Second John, the last years of the apostolic generation in the churches of Asia. It pairs naturally with Second John. There, the elder warns a church not to welcome teachers who deny Christ; here, he rebukes a leader who will not welcome teachers who serve Christ. Together they show a church learning to discern. The wider biblical story of hospitality lies behind it, from Abraham welcoming strangers at Mamre (Genesis 18) to Jesus' words that whoever receives those he sends receives him.
christ: Christ is not named in the letter by title, but he is present in the Name for whose sake the brothers went out (verse 7), a way early Christians referred to Jesus himself. The letter shows what life under that Name looks like: care for strangers, support for the gospel's messengers, and leadership that serves rather than seeks first place. Jesus taught that the greatest must be the servant of all, and Diotrephes' love of being first stands in plain contrast. The elder's standard, that the one who does good is of God (verse 11), echoes the teaching of First John that those born of God show the likeness of the Son.
reading: Read Third John as a real letter between real people, with its gaps and assumptions. Don't build theories on the names. The elder's opening wish that Gaius may prosper and be in good health (verse 2) followed the ordinary conventions of letters in that world, which often began with a wish for the recipient's health. It is a friend's warm greeting, not a promise that the faithful will be wealthy, and reading it as the latter is a common misuse. Notice too how the letter models conflict: the elder names the wrong plainly, plans to address it face to face, and refuses to let one domineering leader define the church.

structure.title: Greeting and joy
structure.summary: The elder greets Gaius, wishes him health, and rejoices at reports that he walks in the truth.

structure.title: Hospitality to the brothers
structure.summary: He commends Gaius for welcoming traveling workers who were strangers to him and urges him to send them on in a manner worthy of God.

structure.title: The problem of Diotrephes
structure.summary: Diotrephes, who loves to be first, rejects the elder's authority, slanders him, refuses the brothers, and expels those who would welcome them.

structure.title: Imitate the good; Demetrius commended
structure.summary: Gaius should imitate the good, not the evil. Demetrius has a good testimony from all and from the truth itself.

structure.title: Closing
structure.summary: The elder hopes to visit soon and speak face to face, and sends and asks for greetings among friends.

themes.title: Hospitality as partnership
themes.body: By welcoming and supplying traveling workers, Gaius becomes a fellow worker for the truth. Hospitality in the early church was not a social nicety but a direct share in mission, and the letter treats it as one of the clearest expressions of love.

themes.title: Walking in the truth
themes.body: The elder's greatest joy is to hear that his children walk in the truth (verse 4). Truth is not only believed but lived, and in this letter it is lived in faithfulness to strangers and generosity to those who serve.

themes.title: The danger of loving first place
themes.body: Diotrephes is the Bible's brief portrait of a leader who treats the church as his own. He rejects outside accountability, controls who may be welcomed, and uses exclusion as a weapon. The letter names the sin plainly and does not excuse it because the man holds a position.

themes.title: Imitation and testimony
themes.body: Believers become like what they imitate. The elder urges Gaius to imitate the good, and he offers Demetrius as someone whose life is confirmed by many witnesses. Character in the church is a matter of public testimony, not private claims.

keyChapters.why: The whole letter: hospitality as partnership in the truth, and a warning against leadership that loves to be first.

parts.body:
3 John is the shortest book in the New Testament by word count: fourteen verses in the BSB, a single sheet of papyrus. It reads aloud in about two minutes. It is the most personal of John's letters, a private note from ‘the elder’ to a friend named Gaius, ‘whom I love in the truth’ (verse 1).

It sets three men side by side. Gaius has welcomed travelling Christian workers, even though they were strangers to him, fed them and sent them on their way. The elder thanks him and urges him to keep doing it, because those who support such workers become ‘fellow workers for the truth’ (verse 8). Diotrephes, a leader in the church, ‘loves to be first’ (verse 9). He has refused the elder's letter, spread malicious talk, turned the travellers away, and put out of the church those who wanted to welcome them. And Demetrius, very likely the man who carried the letter, has ‘a good testimony from everyone’ (verse 12).

Between them stands one sentence that sums up the letter: “Beloved, do not imitate what is evil, but what is good” (verse 11).

The letter is a window onto ordinary church life at the end of the first century: travel, hospitality, money, letters, a church quarrel and a friendship. It shows truth and love not as ideas but as the way believers treat strangers and handle power.

Its opening wish, that Gaius ‘may prosper and enjoy good health’ (verse 2), is one of the most misused verses in the Bible. These notes say plainly what it means and what it does not.

As in 2 John, the writer calls himself ‘the elder’ and gives no name. Early tradition identified him with John the apostle, and the three letters share their words and ideas: truth, love, walking in the truth, testimony, seeing God. So most readers think one writer or one circle stands behind all three.

Some scholars think the elder was a leader distinct from the apostle, perhaps the ‘elder John’ whom Papias named early in the second century. Others hold that the apostle himself, as an old man, used the title. These notes do not choose. The book pages on 1 John and 2 John say more.

What the letter itself makes plain is this. The elder had standing over more than one congregation. He sent out travelling workers, and they reported back to him. He expected his letters and messengers to be received. And at least one local leader was now refusing him.

The church received 3 John more slowly than 1 John. In the early 300s Eusebius listed 2 and 3 John among the books that were disputed but widely known, and the Syriac churches long read a New Testament without them. In the end the church received them as Scripture.

parts.h: Gaius, Diotrephes and Demetrius: what is known
parts.body:
We know nothing of these three men beyond this letter, and it is wise not to build theories on their names.

Gaius was one of the most common Roman names. The New Testament mentions several men called Gaius, in Macedonia, Derbe and Corinth, but there is no good reason to identify this one with any of them. What the letter shows is that he was loved by the elder, faithful to the truth, and generous to strangers.

Diotrephes is a Greek name meaning ‘nourished by Zeus’. Whether he held an office or simply dominated a house church is not clear. Scholars have read his quarrel with the elder as personal ambition, as local leaders resisting a senior leader from outside, or as an early step toward the single presiding bishop found in the second century. The letter describes what he did. It does not describe his office or his motives, beyond the one word that he ‘loves to be first’.

Demetrius ‘has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself’ (verse 12). Verse 12 reads like a letter of recommendation, a common kind of letter in that world, and Demetrius probably carried this one.

parts.h: When, and the world of travel
parts.body:
Like the other letters of John, 3 John is usually dated late in the first century, around AD 85 to 100, and placed in the region of Ephesus. Nothing in it fixes the date more closely. Unlike 1 and 2 John, it shows no sign of a quarrel about who Jesus is. The trouble here is about authority and hospitality.

Christian mission in the Roman world ran on hospitality. Inns were few, expensive, and often had a bad name, so travellers depended on networks of family, friends and patrons. Early Christians built such a network out of their churches. To ‘send them on their way’ (verse 6) meant giving food, money and perhaps company for the next stage of the trip, and it was a recognised Christian duty (Romans 15:24; Titus 3:13).

The workers in this letter ‘went out on behalf of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles’ (verse 7). They did not take support from unbelievers. That set them apart from the many wandering teachers and philosophers of the time who lived on public gifts and were often suspected of preaching for profit. The Didache, a Christian handbook from about the same time or a little later, gives rules for receiving travelling apostles and prophets, which shows how common the system was, and how open to abuse.

3 John follows the ordinary shape of a personal letter of its day more closely than any other book of the New Testament: sender, reader, a wish for good health, joy, the body of the letter, and greetings.

Greeting and joy (verses 1-4). The elder to Gaius. A prayer for his health. Joy that he walks in the truth.

Hospitality to the brothers (verses 5-8). Thanks for welcoming strangers. A request to send them on ‘in a manner worthy of God’.

Diotrephes (verses 9-10). The leader who loves to be first, and what he has done.

Imitate the good; Demetrius (verses 11-12). The moral of the letter, and a word for the man who carries it.

Goodbye (verses 13-14). A hope to visit soon, and greetings between friends.

Notice the three men set side by side, with verse 11 between them. And notice ‘Beloved’, spoken to Gaius four times.

parts.h: ‘That you may prosper and enjoy good health’
parts.body:
“Beloved, I pray that in every way you may prosper and enjoy good health, as your soul also prospers” (verse 2).

Read in its setting, this is a friend's greeting. Surviving papyrus letters from the time regularly open with a prayer or wish for the reader's health, much as a letter today might begin, ‘I hope you are well’. The elder follows that custom, warmly. He prays for his friend's body as well as his soul, and it is right for Christians to do the same: God cares about the whole person.

The word translated ‘prosper’ first meant to have a good road, and so to go well or succeed. It is not a word about money. And the verse is a prayer for one man, not a promise to every Christian.

Yet the verse has often been used to teach that God wills wealth and health for every believer who has enough faith, or who gives enough. This is often called prosperity teaching, or the prosperity gospel. It is one of the things this site does not teach as true. Many who teach it are sincere, and many who believe it are hoping for help in hard times. They deserve care, not scorn. But it is a mistake, and this verse does not support it. The New Testament shows faithful believers who were poor, sick and persecuted, and Jesus warned against the love of money.

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

If you gave money because you were pressed or frightened, or because someone promised that God would pay you back, and the return never came, that was not your failure. You were not lacking in faith. The promise was wrong. It may help to talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If you are in money trouble now, look for a trusted adviser where you live; these notes are not financial advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

“Beloved, you are faithful in what you are doing for the brothers, and especially since they are strangers to you” (verse 5). Gaius had opened his home to people he did not know. They went back to the elder's church and spoke of his love.

The elder asks him to keep doing it: “You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God” (verse 6). ‘In a manner worthy of God’ sets a high standard. Gaius is to treat these travellers as God's own messengers.

Then he gives the reason. “Therefore we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth” (verse 8). The word for ‘fellow workers’ is the one Paul often uses for his co-workers. Those who go and those who send share one work. Gaius never left his town, but by his bread and his bed he became part of the mission.

Hospitality in the early church was not a nicety. It was one of the clearest ways love was lived. And it reached past friends to strangers. Jesus said, “whoever receives the one I send receives Me” (John 13:20).

parts.h: The leader who loves to be first
parts.body:
“I have written to the church about this, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not accept our instruction” (verse 9). The Greek word for ‘loves to be first’ appears only here in the New Testament. It names Diotrephes' fault in one word: the hunger to be in charge.

The elder lists what he has done. He refused the elder's letter, perhaps a letter now lost; some have suggested it was 2 John. He spread ‘malicious slander’. He refused to welcome the travelling workers. And he stopped others from welcoming them, ‘even putting them out of the church’ (verse 10).

This is a short portrait of a leader who treats a church as his own. He will not be accountable to anyone outside. He controls who may be welcomed. He uses exclusion as a weapon. The letter names the wrong plainly and does not excuse it because the man holds a position.

Notice how the elder answers. He does not reply in kind. He plans to come and name what has happened, face to face (verse 10). He does not let one domineering leader define the church. And he points Gaius to a better way: imitate what is good.

It is also worth seeing the contrast with Jesus' teaching. “If anyone wants to be first, he must be the last of all and the servant of all” (Mark 9:35).

If you have been harmed by a controlling leader or church, what was done was wrong, and it was not your fault. Being taken in by someone who seemed godly is not a sign of weak faith; the Corinthians were taken in too. You are free to step away and to tell someone you trust. If you were abused in other ways, or a crime was done, it should be reported to the authorities. A pastor or counsellor outside that church may help you sort out what happened. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

“Beloved, do not imitate what is evil, but what is good. The one who does good is of God; the one who does evil has not seen God” (verse 11).

This verse stands between Diotrephes and Demetrius, and it gives the moral of the letter. People become like what they copy. Gaius has two examples before him. He is to follow the good one.

The second sentence echoes 1 John. Those born of God show the family likeness in what they do. Doing good shows that a person ‘is of God’. Doing evil shows that he ‘has not seen God’, whatever he claims.

Then Demetrius. He has ‘a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself’, and the elder adds his own: ‘you know that our testimony is true’ (verse 12). Character in the church is a matter of open witness, confirmed by many, not private claims.

Jesus is not named by title in this short letter. But he is there. The workers ‘went out on behalf of the Name’ (verse 7). Early Christians spoke of Jesus that way: ‘the Name’ was the name of Jesus, for whose sake they lived and travelled.

The letter shows what life under that Name looks like. It welcomes strangers. It shares what it has. It supports those who carry the message. And it refuses to use power to promote itself. Diotrephes' love of being first is the opposite of the Christ who came to serve. Gaius' open door reflects the Jesus who said that whoever receives those he sends receives him.

3 John does not quote the Old Testament, but its picture of hospitality is old. Abraham saw three strangers by his tent at Mamre and “ran from the entrance of his tent to meet them” (Genesis 18:2). He fed them before he knew who they were. Elijah was fed by a widow at Zarephath, who shared her last flour and oil (1 Kings 17).

The law commanded care for the stranger: “So you also must love the foreigner, since you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 10:19).

‘Prosper’ has its own Old Testament history. The psalm pictures the person who loves God's law as a tree that “prospers in all he does” (Psalm 1:3). That is a picture of a life rooted in God, bearing fruit in season, not a promise of riches. The wisdom books also say, “A good name is more desirable than great riches” (Proverbs 22:1).

And Diotrephes has an ancestor in Korah, who rose against Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16), and a warning in the proverb: “Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18).

It is not a promise of wealth and health to every believer. Verse 2 is a friend's greeting and prayer, in the custom of the time.

It is not a licence for a leader to control who may come and go in a church. It names that as wrong.

It is not a call to open the door to anyone at all, whatever they teach. 2 John, its twin, warns against giving a platform to teachers who deny Christ.

And it is not a dry piece of church business. It is a letter between friends, full of joy at people walking in the truth.

Read it as a real letter between real people, with its gaps and its assumptions. It takes about two minutes aloud.

Read it beside 2 John. In 2 John the elder warns a church not to welcome teachers who deny Christ. In 3 John he rebukes a leader who will not welcome workers who serve Christ, and he thanks a friend who does. Together they show a church learning to tell the difference: neither open to everything nor closed to everyone.

Notice how the elder handles conflict. He names the wrong plainly, plans to address it face to face, and keeps his eye on what is good.

And let it ask its questions. Whom could you welcome? Whose work could you support? Where do you want to be first?

The notes on the chapter go through it passage by passage in plain words.

hard.line: ‘That you may prosper and enjoy good health’: a friend's greeting, not a promise of wealth.
Hospitality to strangers: ‘fellow workers for the truth’.
‘Accepting nothing from the Gentiles’: why the workers took no support from unbelievers.
Diotrephes, ‘who loves to be first’: a leader who treats the church as his own.
‘The one who does evil has not seen God’.

words.line: Greek presbuteros, an older man or a church leader. The writer's title (1:1).
Greek euodoō, first ‘to have a good road’, so to go well. Not a word about money (1:2).
Greek alētheia. Gaius walks in it; the workers serve it (1:3-4, 8).
Greek propempō, to supply a traveller for the next stage of the trip (1:6).
The name of Jesus, for whose sake the workers went out (1:7).
Greek synergos, one who works alongside. Those who support missionaries share their work (1:8).
Greek philoprōteuō, found only here in the New Testament: hunger for first place (1:9).
Greek marturia, open witness to a person's character (1:12).

places.name: Ephesus
places.line: The letter names no place. Early tradition places John's last years here, in the Roman province of Asia, and the church has long linked the letters of John with him there.

teaching.mapNote: 3 John names no place on earth. It does not say where the elder was, or where Gaius lived. Early tradition places John's last years at Ephesus, in the Roman province of Asia, and the letters of John are usually placed in that region, so the map shows Ephesus alone.
